title: Animal rights

definition.text: The philosophy that many or all sentient animals have moral worth apart from their usefulness to people, and that their basic interests, such as avoiding suffering, deserve the same consideration as similar human interests.

facts.text: In its narrow sense, animals have rights to life, liberty and freedom from torture that cannot be overridden by appeals to total welfare.
The argument from marginal cases says that if infants and cognitively disabled people have moral status, animals lacking no relevant trait must too.
The two main philosophical approaches are utilitarian, led by Peter Singer, and rights-based, led by Tom Regan and Gary Francione.
Regan argues animals are 'subjects-of-a-life' and so bearers of rights; Francione argues they need only the right not to be owned.
Unlike animal welfare advocates, who aim to reduce suffering, animal rights supporters often seek to abolish practices such as intensive farming, animal testing and hunting.
Critics such as Carl Cohen argue rights holders must be able to understand duties, which animals cannot.

contested_note: Philosophers such as Frey, Cohen, Posner and Scruton reject the claim that animals hold rights.

title: Commensurability

definition.text: Whether two values share a common measure; incommensurable values have no common standard or cannot be compared in a certain way.

facts.text: Two values such as freedom and security are incommensurable when no amount of one would make up for a loss of the other.
Two options are incomparable when neither is better and they are not exactly equally good.
Commodification makes different things commensurable by giving them a common exchange value in money.
Joseph Raz holds that genuine incomparability exists; Ruth Chang proposes a fourth relation, 'parity'; John Broome treats incomparability as vagueness.
Incomparability troubles consequentialism, since if outcomes cannot be compared neither action may be better.

contested_note: Philosophers disagree whether apparent incomparability is real, mere ignorance, parity or vagueness.

definition.text: An argument that two options are incomparable: if a tiny gain to one does not make it better than the other, they cannot have been exactly equal.

facts.text: In the example, adding 5 cents a year to a banking job should not tip the choice against a professor's job if the two are too different to compare.
The three ordinary comparisons, in Ruth Chang's terms, are better, worse and equally good.

definition.text: Karl Polanyi's term for things treated as market commodities though not made for sale: land, labour and money.

facts.text: It comes from Polanyi's 1944 book The Great Transformation.
Before markets ordered society, land, labour and money were embedded in social relations and governed by morals, religion and community.
Treating public goods and social necessities as commodities rather than protected rights may destabilise social systems.
Because nature originates outside capitalist production, its value cannot be fully counted in money, which tends towards overexploitation.
Resistance to treating the environment as a market good is seen as Polanyi's 'double movement' of forces for and against markets.
